statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field $k$ with a [basis](c:basis) $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ indexed by a totally ordered set $I$. Then the ordered monomials $x_{i_1} \cdots x_{i_n}$ with $i_1 \le \dots \le i_n$ and $n \ge 0$ form a basis of the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) $U(\mathfrak g)$.

hypotheses.text: The space $\mathfrak g$ is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field $k$.
The $k$-vector space $\mathfrak g$ has a [basis](c:basis) $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ with $I$ totally ordered.

conclusion: The ordered monomials, with the empty monomial $1$, are a $k$-basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$.

proofs.name: Polynomial module
proofs.slogan: Reorder monomials to span the algebra, then let it act on a polynomial ring to prove that the ordered monomials are independent.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem over a field of any characteristic and for any index set. Step 1 gives spanning; steps 2 to 4 give independence.

roles.why: The bracket reorders products, and the Jacobi identity makes the action on the polynomial ring respect the relations.
The ordered basis names the ordered monomials and the variables $z_i$ of the polynomial ring.

steps.slogan: Reorder every monomial into ordered monomials plus shorter monomials.
steps.detail: $U(\mathfrak g)$ is a quotient of the [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra), so it is spanned by monomials in the $x_i$. Since $x_j x_i = x_i x_j + [x_j, x_i]$ and the bracket is a combination of the $x_k$, a monomial of length $n$ equals an ordered monomial plus monomials of length below $n$. Induction on $n$ shows that the ordered monomials span.

steps.slogan: Define the action of each $x_i$ on the polynomial ring $k[z_j]$ by recursion on degree.
steps.detail: Let $S = k[z_j]_{j \in I}$ be the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring). If $i$ is at most every index in the monomial $z_J$, put $x_i \cdot z_J = z_i z_J$. Otherwise write $z_J = z_j z_{J'}$ with $j < i$ the smallest index and put $x_i \cdot z_J = x_j \cdot (x_i \cdot z_{J'}) + [x_i, x_j] \cdot z_{J'}$, which uses only lower degrees.

steps.slogan: Check that the defined action satisfies $x_i x_j - x_j x_i = [x_i, x_j]$.
steps.detail: By induction on the degree of the monomial, the case where the smaller of $i, j$ is at most every index of the monomial follows from the definition. The remaining case reduces, through the recursion, to the Jacobi identity for $x_i$, $x_j$ and $x_k$. So $\mathfrak g$ acts on $S$ as a Lie algebra.

steps.slogan: Map ordered monomials to distinct monomials of $S$ to prove independence.
steps.detail: By the universal property, the action gives an algebra map $U(\mathfrak g) \to \operatorname{End}(S)$. For $i_1 \le \dots \le i_n$, applying the first rule from the right gives $x_{i_1} \cdots x_{i_n} \cdot 1 = z_{i_1} \cdots z_{i_n}$. These monomials of $S$ are independent, so a vanishing combination of ordered monomials has zero coefficients.

steps.slogan: Join spanning and independence to get a basis.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that the ordered monomials span $U(\mathfrak g)$. Step 4 shows that they are linearly independent. Together they form a basis.

concepts.c:lie-algebra: The bracket of the Lie algebra drives both reordering and the module structure.
concepts.c:basis: The ordered basis defines the ordered monomials and the variables $z_i$.
concepts.c:universal-enveloping-algebra: The algebra whose basis is the object of the theorem.
concepts.c:tensor-algebra: Monomials in the $x_i$ span the tensor algebra, and so its quotient.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The polynomial ring is the module on which independence is tested.

source.note: The classical proof by a representation on the polynomial ring, as in Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory, sections 17.3 and 17.4 (Lemma 17.4 A).

statement: If $f$ and $g$ are real functions defined near $a$ and [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at $a$, then $fg$ is differentiable at $a$ and $(fg)'(a) = f'(a)\,g(a) + f(a)\,g'(a)$.
conclusion: The [derivative](c:derivative) of $fg$ at $a$ exists and equals $f'(a)\,g(a) + f(a)\,g'(a)$.

proofs.name: Split the difference quotient
proofs.slogan: Split the difference quotient of $fg$ into two quotients, then take limits with the continuity of $g$.
proofs.scope: Differentiability at one point $a$; for functions on a set $X$, apply it at every point. Steps 2 and 3 give the limit of the two terms.

roles.why: The quotient of $f$ has the limit $f'(a)$, which gives the first term.
The quotient of $g$ has the limit $g'(a)$, and it makes $g$ continuous at $a$.

steps.slogan: Split the difference quotient of $fg$ by adding and subtracting $f(a)g(x)$.
steps.detail: For $x \ne a$ near $a$, $\frac{f(x)g(x) - f(a)g(a)}{x - a} = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}\, g(x) + f(a)\, \frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}$. This is an identity of real numbers, checked by expanding the right side.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ is continuous at $a$.
steps.detail: Write $g(x) - g(a) = \frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}\,(x - a)$. As $x \to a$ the quotient tends to $g'(a)$ and $x - a$ tends to $0$, so the product tends to $0$. Hence $g(x) \to g(a)$.

steps.slogan: Take the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) of each term with the limit laws.
steps.detail: The first quotient tends to $f'(a)$ and $g(x)$ tends to $g(a)$ by step 2, so the first term tends to $f'(a)\,g(a)$. The second quotient tends to $g'(a)$, so the second term tends to $f(a)\,g'(a)$. A limit of a sum is the sum of the limits.

steps.slogan: Read the limit as the derivative of $fg$ at $a$.
steps.detail: The difference quotient of $fg$ at $a$ has the limit $f'(a)\,g(a) + f(a)\,g'(a)$. By the definition of the derivative, $fg$ is differentiable at $a$ with this derivative.

concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability gives the limits of the two difference quotients.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient that the proof computes.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: The limit laws turn the split quotient into the formula.

source.note: The classical proof, as in Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, theorem 5.3(b).

statement: A [pseudorandom generator](c:pseudorandom-generator) that stretches $n$ bits to more than $n$ bits exists if and only if a [one-way function](c:one-way-function) exists.

hypotheses.text: The generator and the function are polynomial-time algorithms, and security is against probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries.

conclusion: Pseudorandom generators exist exactly when one-way functions exist.

new_concepts.name: pseudorandom generator
new_concepts.reminder: A pseudorandom generator is an efficient map that stretches a short random seed into a longer string that no efficient test tells from random.
new_concepts.definition: An efficiently computable map $G\colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}$ with $\ell(n) > n$ such that no probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm distinguishes $G(s)$, for a uniform seed $s$, from a uniform string of length $\ell(n)$ with non-negligible advantage.

proofs.name: Smoothing entropy with hashing
proofs.slogan: A generator is a one-way function; conversely, extract and smooth the entropy of one iteration of the function with universal hashing.
proofs.scope: An outline of the cited proof. The easy direction is proved here; steps 2 to 4 rest on the work of Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby.

roles.why: Every reduction turns an efficient adversary into an efficient inverter or distinguisher.

steps.slogan: Show that every pseudorandom generator is a one-way function.
steps.detail: Iterate the generator to reach stretch $2n$ (a hybrid argument). If an efficient $A$ inverts $G$ with probability $\varepsilon(n)$, the test that accepts $y$ when $G(A(y)) = y$ accepts $G(s)$ with probability at least $\varepsilon(n)$ and a uniform $y$ with probability at most $2^{-n}$. So $\varepsilon$ is negligible.

steps.slogan: Build a function whose output only looks as if it has more entropy than its input.
steps.detail: From a [one-way function](c:one-way-function) $f$, the cited work combines $f(x)$ with hash values of $x$ under a universal hash function $h$. A [hard-core](c:hard-core-predicate) argument, in the style of Goldreich and Levin, shows that no efficient test sees how much entropy this output really has.

steps.slogan: Smooth the entropy by taking many independent copies of the construction.
steps.detail: The output entropy is not flat. The cited work takes many independent copies of the construction. By the law of large numbers, the joint output is close to a flat distribution on a typical set.

steps.slogan: Extract nearly uniform bits from the flattened output with a universal hash.
steps.detail: Apply a universal hash function with a fresh key to the flattened output. The leftover hash lemma makes the result close to uniform, and the pseudo-entropy surplus makes it longer than the seed and the key together.

steps.slogan: Join both directions and amplify the stretch to any polynomial length.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives a one-way function from a generator. Steps 2 to 4 give a generator that stretches by at least one bit from a one-way function. Iterating that generator gives every polynomial stretch, which proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:pseudorandom-generator: The generator is the object that exists exactly when a one-way function exists.
concepts.c:one-way-function: The one-way function is the hard problem that both directions connect to.
concepts.c:hard-core-predicate: Hard-core bits supply the computational unpredictability behind the pseudo-entropy.

source.ref: J. Håstad, R. Impagliazzo, L. A. Levin and M. Luby, A pseudorandom generator from any one-way function, SIAM Journal on Computing 28 (1999), no. 4, 1364-1396
source.note: The full construction and its security proof; a simplified account is in Haitner, Reingold and Vadhan, Efficiency improvements in constructing pseudorandom generators from one-way functions.

statement: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field) with $2 \ne 0$ and let $a, b, c \in K$ with $a \ne 0$. Put $D = b^2 - 4ac$. The [polynomial](c:polynomial) $ax^2 + bx + c$ has a root in $K$ if and only if $D$ is a square $s^2$ in $K$, and its roots are exactly $x = \frac{-b \pm s}{2a}$.
conclusion: The roots are exactly $x = (-b \pm s)/(2a)$ with $s^2 = D$, and there is no root if $D$ is not a [square](c:square-root) in $K$.

proofs.name: Completing the square
proofs.slogan: Multiply by $4a$, complete the square, take square roots and solve for $x$.
proofs.scope: Every field with $2 \ne 0$. Over the reals, $s = \sqrt D$ exists exactly when $D \ge 0$; over the complex numbers it always exists.

roles.why: A field has no zero divisors, and $2 \ne 0$ makes $2a$ and $4a$ invertible.
With $a \ne 0$ the factor $4a$ is invertible, so no root is lost or added.

steps.slogan: Multiply the equation by the invertible element $4a$.
steps.detail:
Since $a 
e 0$ and $2 
e 0$, $4a 
e 0$ in the field $K$. So $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ holds if and only if $4a^2x^2 + 4abx + 4ac = 0$.

steps.slogan: [Complete the square](c:completing-the-square) to write the equation as $(2ax+b)^2 = D$.
steps.detail: We have $4a^2x^2 + 4abx = (2ax + b)^2 - b^2$. So the equation of step 1 is equivalent to $(2ax + b)^2 = b^2 - 4ac = D$.

steps.slogan: Take square roots: $u^2 = s^2$ holds if and only if $u = \pm s$.
steps.detail: $u^2 = s^2$ means $(u - s)(u + s) = 0$. A field has no zero divisors, so $u = s$ or $u = -s$. If $D$ is not a [square](c:square-root) in $K$, no $u$ has $u^2 = D$, so there is no root.

steps.slogan: Solve $2ax + b = \pm s$ for $x$ by dividing by $2a$.
steps.detail: Since $2a \ne 0$, the equation $2ax + b = \pm s$ gives $x = (-b \pm s)/(2a)$. Every step above is reversible, so each such $x$ is a root.

concepts.c:field: The field structure gives division and the absence of zero divisors.
concepts.c:polynomial: The theorem finds the roots of a degree two polynomial.
concepts.c:square-root: The roots exist exactly when the discriminant has a square root.
concepts.c:completing-the-square: Completing the square turns the quadratic into a perfect square equation.

source.note: The classical derivation by completing the square, valid over any field of characteristic not 2.

statement: There is a constant $p_0 > 0$ such that, for every noise rate $p < p_0$, every quantum circuit of size $T$ is simulated, to accuracy $\varepsilon$, by a circuit of size $T\,\mathrm{polylog}(T/\varepsilon)$ that works when each of its operations suffers local noise of strength $p$.

hypotheses.text: Each gate, preparation and measurement of the simulating circuit fails with probability at most $p$, in a local stochastic way.
The noise rate $p$ is below the threshold $p_0$.
The ideal circuit has size $T$ and the target accuracy is $\varepsilon > 0$.

conclusion: A noisy circuit of size $T\,\mathrm{polylog}(T/\varepsilon)$ has an output within $\varepsilon$ of the ideal output.

proofs.name: Concatenated codes
proofs.slogan: Encode in an error-correcting code with fault-tolerant gadgets, concatenate it, and watch the logical error rate fall doubly exponentially.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; steps 2 and 3 rest on the cited work. The threshold $p_0 = 1/A$ depends on the gadgets.

roles.why: Local noise keeps faults in different gadgets independent enough for the counting of step 3.
A rate below $1/A$ makes the recursion $p \mapsto Ap^2$ contract to zero.
The size $T$ and accuracy $\varepsilon$ fix the number of levels and the final size.

steps.slogan: Encode every qubit in a small [error-correcting code](c:error-correcting-code) that corrects one error.
steps.detail: Fix a code that corrects any single error in a block. Replace each qubit by a block of this code and each gate, preparation and measurement by an encoded version.

steps.slogan: Make each gadget fault tolerant, so that one fault leaves at most one error per block.
steps.detail: The cited work designs gadgets for a universal gate set, each followed by error correction, such that a single fault spreads to at most one error in each output block. The next correction step then removes it, so a gadget fails only after two faults.

steps.slogan: Bound the failure rate of an encoded operation by $Ap^2$.
steps.detail: A gadget has at most a constant number of locations, so the probability of two faults in it is at most $Ap^2$ for a constant $A$. The encoded circuit is again a noisy circuit with local noise of rate $p_1 \le Ap^2$.

steps.slogan: Concatenate the construction $k$ times to get a [concatenated code](c:concatenated-code) with rate $p_k \le (Ap)^{2^k}/A$.
steps.detail: Applying step 3 to the simulated circuit again gives $p_{j+1} \le Ap_j^2$, so $Ap_k \le (Ap)^{2^k}$ by induction. For $p < p_0 = 1/A$ the rate falls doubly exponentially in $k$.

steps.slogan: Choose the level $k$ for accuracy $\varepsilon$ and count the size.
steps.detail: A circuit with $T$ locations fails with probability at most $Tp_k$, so $k = O(\log\log(T/\varepsilon))$ levels give $Tp_k \le \varepsilon$. Each level multiplies the size by a constant $c$, so the final size is $T c^k = T\,\mathrm{polylog}(T/\varepsilon)$.

concepts.c:error-correcting-code: The code protects each logical qubit against a single fault.
concepts.c:concatenated-code: Repeating the code inside itself squares the error rate at each level.

source.ref: D. Aharonov and M. Ben-Or, Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant error rate, SIAM Journal on Computing 38 (2008), no. 4 (conference version: STOC 1997)
source.note: Also proved independently by Kitaev (Russian Mathematical Surveys 52 (1997)) and by Knill, Laflamme and Zurek (Science 279 (1998)).

statement: Any family of $d + 2$ points $x_1, \dots, x_{d+2}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an index set $I$ such that the [convex hulls](c:convex-hull) of $\{x_i : i \in I\}$ and of $\{x_i : i \notin I\}$ intersect.

hypotheses.text: The family consists of $d + 2$ points $x_1, \dots, x_{d+2}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$.

conclusion: A point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in both [convex hulls](c:convex-hull) (a Radon point).

formal.difference: The declaration states the theorem for any affinely dependent family in a vector space over a linearly ordered field. The $d + 2$ points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ are affinely dependent by the separate lemma finrank_vectorSpan_le_iff_not_affineIndependent.

proofs.name: Affine dependence split by sign
proofs.slogan: Take a nontrivial affine dependence, split its coefficients by sign, and read the common point as a weighted average.
proofs.scope: Every $d \ge 0$; repeated points are allowed because the points form a family. The proof uses only that the family is affinely dependent.

roles.why: There are $d + 2$ points but only $d + 1$ linear conditions, so a nontrivial dependence exists.

steps.slogan: Find a nonzero solution of $\sum \lambda_i x_i = 0$ and $\sum \lambda_i = 0$.
steps.detail: The two conditions are $d + 1$ linear equations in the $d + 2$ unknowns $\lambda_i$. A homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations has a nonzero solution. So the family is not [affinely independent](c:affine-independence).

steps.slogan: Split the indices by the sign of $\lambda_i$ into $I$ and $J$.
steps.detail: Let $I = \{i : \lambda_i \ge 0\}$ and $J = \{i : \lambda_i < 0\}$, so $J$ is the complement of $I$. Some $\lambda_i$ is nonzero and the sum is zero, so some $\lambda_i$ is positive, and $S = \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i > 0$. Also $\sum_{j \in J} \lambda_j = -S$.

steps.slogan: Define $p = \sum_{i \in I} (\lambda_i / S)\, x_i$ and show that the $J$ part gives the same $p$.
steps.detail: From $\sum \lambda_i x_i = 0$ we get $\sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i x_i = \sum_{j \in J} (-\lambda_j)\, x_j$. Dividing by $S$ gives $p = \sum_{j \in J} (-\lambda_j / S)\, x_j$.

steps.slogan: Read both formulas for $p$ as convex combinations to place $p$ in both hulls.
steps.detail: In each formula the coefficients are nonnegative and add to $1$. So $p$ is a convex combination of the $x_i$ with $i \in I$ and of the $x_j$ with $j \in J$. Hence $p$ lies in both [convex hulls](c:convex-hull).

concepts.c:convex-hull: The convex hull is the set of convex combinations where the two parts must meet.
concepts.c:affine-independence: The count of points forces affine dependence, which supplies the coefficients.

source.note: mathlib turns affine dependence into weights (affineIndependent_iff), splits the support by the sign of the weights, takes p as the centerMass of the nonnegative part, and places p in both hulls with centerMass_mem_convexHull and centerMass_mem_convexHull_of_nonpos.

statement: Row insertion defines a bijection from $m \times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) $A$ of nonnegative integers to pairs $(P, Q)$ of [semistandard Young tableaux](c:semistandard-young-tableau) of the same shape. The tableau $P$ has entries in $\{1..n\}$ with content the column sums of $A$, and $Q$ has entries in $\{1..m\}$ with content the row sums.

hypotheses.text: $A = (a_{ij})$ is an $m \times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) with entries in $\mathbb{N}$.

conclusion: The map $A \mapsto (P, Q)$ is a bijection onto the pairs of semistandard tableaux of equal shape with these entry ranges.

proofs.name: Row insertion and reverse bumping
proofs.slogan: Insert the columns of the sorted two-line array into $P$, record the rows in $Q$, and undo the last insertion by reverse bumping.
proofs.scope: The matrix form. A [permutation](c:permutation) matrix gives [standard tableaux](c:standard-young-tableau), the Robinson-Schensted correspondence for permutations. Step 4 builds the inverse, so bijectivity is proved.

roles.why: The entries $a_{ij}$ say how often each pair $(i, j)$ enters the two-line array.

steps.slogan: Turn the matrix into a lexicographically ordered two-line array.
steps.detail: List the pair $(i, j)$ exactly $a_{ij}$ times, sorted by $i$ first and $j$ second: $(i_1, j_1), \dots, (i_N, j_N)$. The array determines $A$ and conversely. The $i_k$ never decrease, and equal $i_k$ have nondecreasing $j_k$.

steps.slogan: Build $P$ by row insertion of $j_k$ and $Q$ by recording $i_k$ in the new box.
steps.detail: To insert $x$ into a row, replace the leftmost entry larger than $x$, or append $x$ if there is none, and insert the replaced entry into the next row. The result is a semistandard tableau with one new box. Put $i_k$ into the same box of $Q$; the contents of $P$ and $Q$ are the $j$'s and the $i$'s.

steps.slogan: Show with the row bumping lemma that $Q$ is semistandard.
steps.detail: If $x \le x'$, the box added by inserting $x'$ right after $x$ lies strictly right of, and weakly above, the box of $x$. Equal $i_k$ come with nondecreasing $j_k$, so they lie in different columns. Since the $i_k$ never decrease, $Q$ has weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns.

steps.slogan: Build the inverse by reverse bumping from the last box of $Q$.
steps.detail: Given $(P, Q)$, take the box of $Q$ with the largest entry, the rightmost one if entries tie. Remove the entry of $P$ in that box and move up: in each row, replace the rightmost entry smaller than the carried entry by it, and carry the replaced one on. The entry leaving row 1 is $j_N$, and the removed entry of $Q$ is $i_N$.

steps.slogan: Show that insertion and reverse bumping undo each other.
steps.detail: By step 3 the box of the last insertion is the rightmost largest box of $Q$, and reverse bumping undoes a row insertion at the box it created. Induction on the number of boxes recovers the array, so the map is injective. The reverse bumping lemma makes the extracted pairs lexicographically ordered, so every pair $(P, Q)$ is reached.

concepts.c:matrix: The matrix is the input that the two-line array encodes.
concepts.c:semistandard-young-tableau: The pair $(P, Q)$ consists of these tableaux, whose shape the insertion tracks.
concepts.c:permutation: Permutation matrices give the classical correspondence with standard tableaux.
concepts.c:standard-young-tableau: Standard tableaux are the semistandard ones that arise from permutations.

source.note: The standard proof, as in Fulton, Young Tableaux (1997), section 4.1, and Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, volume 2, section 7.11.

statement: Let $F(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ be a [Boolean function](c:boolean-function) and $x = x_i$ a variable. Then $F = x \cdot F_x + x' \cdot F_{x'}$, where $F_x$ and $F_{x'}$ are $F$ with $x$ set to $1$ and to $0$, and $+$, $\cdot$, $'$ are the OR, AND and NOT of the [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) of such functions.

hypotheses.text: $x = x_i$ is one of the variables of $F$.

conclusion: The functions $F$ and $x \cdot F_x + x' \cdot F_{x'}$ have the same value at every assignment.

proofs.name: Split on the value of the variable
proofs.slogan: Compare both sides at every assignment, separately for the two values of $x$.
proofs.scope: Every Boolean function and every variable. Two Boolean functions are equal when they agree at all $2^n$ assignments.

roles.why: A Boolean function has a value at every assignment, so equality can be checked point by point.
The variable takes the value $0$ or $1$, which gives the two cases.

steps.slogan: Define the two cofactors by fixing $x_i$ to a constant.
steps.detail: Put $F_x(a) = F(a_1, \dots, a_{i-1}, 1, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_n)$ and $F_{x'}(a)$ the same with $0$ in place $i$. Both are Boolean functions that do not depend on $a_i$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the right side at an assignment with $a_i = 1$.
steps.detail: Then $x = 1$ and $x' = 0$, so $x \cdot F_x + x' \cdot F_{x'}$ equals $F_x(a)$. Setting $x_i$ to $1$ does not change $a$, so $F_x(a) = F(a)$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the right side at an assignment with $a_i = 0$.
steps.detail: Then $x = 0$ and $x' = 1$, so the right side equals $F_{x'}(a)$. Setting $x_i$ to $0$ does not change $a$, so $F_{x'}(a) = F(a)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases to compare the functions at every assignment.
steps.detail: Every assignment has $a_i = 1$ or $a_i = 0$. In both cases the right side equals $F(a)$, so the two functions agree everywhere and are equal.

concepts.c:boolean-function: The identity is checked on a function with finitely many assignments.
concepts.c:boolean-algebra: OR, AND and NOT of functions obey the laws used in the evaluation.

source.note: The direct case check on the value of the variable; the identity is Boole's expansion theorem, also called Shannon's expansion.

statement: Let $S$ be a [separable metric space](c:separable-metric-space) and $\mu_n, \mu$ be [probability measures](c:probability-measure) on $S$ with $\mu_n \to \mu$ [weakly](c:weak-convergence). Then some probability space carries [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_n, X$ with laws $\mu_n, \mu$ and $X_n \to X$ [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence).

hypotheses.text: The space $S$ is a [separable metric space](c:separable-metric-space).

conclusion: There are random variables $X_n$ and $X$ on one probability space with laws $\mu_n$ and $\mu$, and $X_n \to X$ almost surely.

proofs.name: Coupling through small cells
proofs.slogan: Partition the space into small continuity cells, couple all laws to the limit cell by cell, and apply Borel-Cantelli.
proofs.scope: An outline of the cited proof; steps 2 and 3 rest on the cited work. The argument needs only that $\mu$ has separable support.

roles.why: Separability gives countable partitions into cells of small diameter that are continuity sets.
Weak convergence gives convergence of the masses of the continuity cells.

steps.slogan: Partition $S$ into small cells that are continuity sets of $\mu$.
steps.detail: For each $k$ the cited work takes a countable partition of $S$ into sets of diameter below $2^{-k}$ whose boundaries have $\mu$-measure zero, each level refining the previous one. Balls around points of a countable dense set have such boundaries for all but countably many radii.

steps.slogan: Use weak convergence to compare the cell masses of $\mu_n$ and $\mu$.
steps.detail: For a continuity set $B$ of $\mu$, weak convergence gives $\mu_n(B) \to \mu(B)$. So for each $k$ there is $N_k$ such that every $n \ge N_k$ has $\mu_n(B) \ge (1 - 2^{-k})\,\mu(B)$ for the finitely many cells that carry almost all the mass.

steps.slogan: Build $X$ and all $X_n$ from common random numbers with matching cells on large events.
steps.detail: The cited work builds $X \sim \mu$ and each $X_n \sim \mu_n$ from one uniform variable. On an event $G_k$ with $P(G_k^c) \le 2^{-k}$ that does not depend on $n$, $X_n$ and $X$ lie in the same level $k$ cell for all $n \ge N_k$.

steps.slogan: Apply Borel-Cantelli to the events $G_k^c$ to get almost sure convergence.
steps.detail: Since $\sum 2^{-k} < \infty$, almost every $\omega$ lies in $G_k$ for all large $k$. For such $\omega$ and $n \ge N_k$ we have $d(X_n(\omega), X(\omega)) < 2^{-k}$, so $X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega)$.

concepts.c:separable-metric-space: A countable dense set gives the partitions into small cells.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The laws $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ are the measures being realized on one space.
concepts.c:weak-convergence: Convergence of masses of continuity sets is the form of weak convergence used.
concepts.c:random-variable: The random variables $X_n$ and $X$ are the output of the coupling.
concepts.c:almost-sure-convergence: The Borel-Cantelli step turns the cell matching into almost sure convergence.

source.ref: P. Billingsley, Convergence of Probability Measures, 2nd edition, Wiley, 1999, Theorem 6.7
source.note: Skorokhod proved the theorem for complete separable spaces (1956), and Dudley extended it to separable metric spaces: R. M. Dudley, Distances of probability measures and random variables, Annals of Mathematical Statistics 39 (1968), 1563-1572.

statement: Let $f, g, h$ be real functions with $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ for all $x \ne a$ near $a$. If $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$.

hypotheses.text: The [inequality](c:inequality) $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ holds for all $x \ne a$ near $a$.

formal.difference: The declaration works for filters on any domain and values in an order topology, and it assumes the inequalities everywhere. The version with inequalities that hold only eventually is the primed declaration tendsto_of_tendsto_of_tendsto_of_le_of_le'.

proofs.name: Trap the function in an interval
proofs.slogan: Fix an interval around $L$, pick one closeness for $g$, $h$ and the sandwich, and trap $f$ between $g$ and $h$ inside the interval.
proofs.scope: Real functions near a point $a$; the same argument works for one-sided limits and for limits at infinity.

roles.why: The inequality puts $f(x)$ between $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ near $a$.
The limit of $g$ keeps $g(x)$ above $L - \varepsilon$ near $a$.
The limit of $h$ keeps $h(x)$ below $L + \varepsilon$ near $a$.

steps.slogan: Fix an arbitrary interval $(L - \varepsilon, L + \varepsilon)$ around $L$.
steps.detail: Every neighborhood of $L$ contains such an interval. So it is enough to show that, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $f(x)$ lies in this interval for all $x \ne a$ close to $a$.

steps.slogan: Choose one closeness $\delta$ that controls $g$, $h$ and the sandwich at once.
steps.detail: The two limits give $\delta_1, \delta_2 > 0$ with $|g(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ when $0 < |x - a| < \delta_1$ and $|h(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ when $0 < |x - a| < \delta_2$. The sandwich holds for $0 < |x - a| < \delta_3$. Let $\delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2, \delta_3)$.

steps.slogan: Trap $f(x)$ between $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ inside the interval.
steps.detail: For $0 < |x - a| < \delta$ we get $L - \varepsilon < g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x) < L + \varepsilon$. The sandwich is used only here, to pass from the bounds on $g$ and $h$ to a bound on $f$.

steps.slogan: Read the bound as the definition of the limit of $f$.
steps.detail: The chain gives $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $0 < |x - a| < \delta$. Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$.

concepts.c:inequality: The inequality $g \le f \le h$ traps $f$ between two controlled functions.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: The limits of $g$ and $h$ bound both near $L$; the limit of $f$ follows.

source.note: mathlib reduces to the eventual version, which shows that the intervals Icc (g x) (h x) shrink into every neighborhood of the limit (Filter.Tendsto.Icc, Filter.Tendsto.of_smallSets) and that f x lies in them.

statement: Let $E/F$ be a [field extension](c:field-extension). Then $E$ is algebraic over $F$ and generated by one element, a [primitive element](c:primitive-element), if and only if $E/F$ has only finitely many [intermediate fields](c:intermediate-field).
conclusion: $E = F(\alpha)$ for an algebraic $\alpha$ exactly when the set of intermediate fields between $F$ and $E$ is finite.

proofs.name: Divisors of the minimal polynomial
proofs.slogan: A simple extension has finitely many intermediate fields by monic divisors; conversely, finitely many fields force algebraicity, finiteness and a primitive element.
proofs.scope: Both directions, for finite and infinite $F$. The catalog's source text names the unrelated Steinitz theorem on polyhedra; this record follows the linked mathlib declaration, Steinitz's field theorem.

roles.why: The extension supplies the intermediate fields and the minimal polynomials in both directions.

steps.slogan: Attach to each intermediate field $K$ a monic divisor of the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $\alpha$.
steps.detail: Let $E = F(\alpha)$ with $\alpha$ algebraic, and let $m$ be its minimal polynomial over $F$. For an intermediate field $K$, the minimal polynomial $g_K$ of $\alpha$ over $K$ is monic and divides $m$ in $E[x]$.

steps.slogan: Recover $K$ as the field generated by the coefficients of $g_K$.
steps.detail: Let $K'$ be generated over $F$ by the coefficients of $g_K$, so $K' \subseteq K$. The polynomial $g_K$ is irreducible over $K'$ because it is irreducible over $K$, so $[E : K'] = \deg g_K = [E : K]$ and $K' = K$. Since $m$ has finitely many monic divisors in $E[x]$, there are finitely many $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that finitely many intermediate fields force every element to be algebraic.
steps.detail: For $\alpha \in E$ the fields $F(\alpha^n)$ with $n \ge 1$ cannot all differ, so $F(\alpha^m) = F(\alpha^n)$ with $m < n$. If $\alpha$ were transcendental, $[F(\alpha) : F(\alpha^n)] = n$ would make these fields differ. So $\alpha$ is algebraic.

steps.slogan: Show that $E$ is a finite extension of $F$.
steps.detail: $E$ is the union of the fields $F(x)$ for $x \in E$, and only finitely many of them exist. Each is finite over $F$ because $x$ is algebraic. The join of finitely many finite extensions is finite, so $[E : F] < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Produce a primitive element, for finite and for infinite $F$ separately.
steps.detail: If $F$ is finite, $E$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field) whose [cyclic](c:cyclic-group) multiplicative group has a generator $\alpha$, so $E = F(\alpha)$. If $F$ is infinite and $a, b \in E$, two values $c \ne c'$ in $F$ give $F(a + cb) = F(a + c'b)$ by finiteness, so $b$ and then $a$ lie in this field and $F(a, b)$ is simple. Induction over generators gives $E = F(\alpha)$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions to prove the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives finitely many intermediate fields from a primitive element. Steps 3 to 5 give a primitive element from finitely many intermediate fields. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:field-extension: The theorem compares one extension with the family of fields inside it.
concepts.c:primitive-element: A primitive element is the single generator of the extension.
concepts.c:intermediate-field: Intermediate fields are the objects counted, and each is determined by a polynomial.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: Its monic divisors form the finite list that indexes the intermediate fields.
concepts.c:finite-field: Over a finite base, the extension is a finite field with a generator.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: The multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic, and a generator is primitive.

source.note: mathlib proves the forward direction by injecting intermediate fields into monic divisors of the minimal polynomial (finite_intermediateField_of_exists_primitive_element) and the converse with isAlgebraic_of_finite_intermediateField, FiniteDimensional.of_finite_intermediateField and exists_primitive_element_of_finite_intermediateField.

statement: Let $x \ne 1$ be an element of a [division ring](c:division-ring), for example a field, and let $m \le n$ be natural numbers. Then $\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} x^i = \frac{x^n - x^m}{x - 1}$.

hypotheses.text: The element $x$ lies in a [division ring](c:division-ring), for example a field.

conclusion: The [geometric series](c:geometric-series) segment $\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} x^i$ equals $(x^n - x^m)/(x - 1)$.

proofs.name: Telescoping from zero
proofs.slogan: Sum the powers from zero by telescoping, divide by $x - 1$, and subtract two initial sums.
proofs.scope: All $m \le n$, including the empty sum $m = n$. The division is legal because $x - 1 \ne 0$.

roles.why: The ring has inverses of nonzero elements, and $x - 1$ commutes with powers of $x$.
The element $x - 1$ is nonzero, so it is invertible.
With $m \le n$ the sum over $m \le i < n$ is a difference of initial sums.

steps.slogan: Multiply the initial sum by $x - 1$ and telescope.
steps.detail: $(x - 1)\sum_{i<n} x^i = \sum_{i<n} (x^{i+1} - x^i) = x^n - 1$, because consecutive terms cancel.

steps.slogan: Divide by $x - 1$, which is invertible because $x \ne 1$.
steps.detail: In a division ring the nonzero element $x - 1$ has an inverse. So $\sum_{i<n} x^i = (x^n - 1)/(x - 1)$ for every $n$, also for $n = 0$ where both sides are $0$.

steps.slogan: Write the [finite sum](c:finite-sum) over $m \le i < n$ as a difference of initial sums.
steps.detail: Since $m \le n$, $\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} x^i = \sum_{i<n} x^i - \sum_{i<m} x^i$. The terms with $i < m$ occur in both initial sums and cancel.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two quotients over the common denominator $x - 1$.
steps.detail: By step 2, the difference is $\frac{x^n - 1}{x - 1} - \frac{x^m - 1}{x - 1} = \frac{x^n - x^m}{x - 1}$.

concepts.c:division-ring: Division by the nonzero element $x - 1$ needs a division ring.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The sum of consecutive powers is the object of the formula.
concepts.c:finite-sum: The sum over a range splits as a difference of two initial sums.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the sum over Finset.Ico m n as a difference of sums over range (Finset.sum_Ico_eq_sub) and applies geom_sum_eq to each.

statement: In a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) $X$, an [analytic set](c:analytic-set) $s$ whose complement is also analytic is a [Borel set](c:borel-set).

formal.difference: The declaration concludes that $s$ is measurable for any $\sigma$-algebra that contains the open sets. The Borel $\sigma$-algebra is the smallest such $\sigma$-algebra.

proofs.name: Separate the set from its complement
proofs.slogan: Separate the analytic set from its analytic complement by a Borel set, and show that this Borel set equals the set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The Lusin separation theorem is used as a known result, and the rest is a short argument about sets.

roles.why: Distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods, which the separation theorem needs.
The set $s$ is one of the two disjoint analytic sets to separate.
The complement is the other disjoint analytic set to separate.

steps.slogan: Observe that $s$ and $s^c$ are disjoint analytic sets.
steps.detail: By hypothesis $s$ and $s^c$ are [analytic](c:analytic-set), and $s \cap s^c = \emptyset$. So the pair $(s, s^c)$ meets the hypotheses of the Lusin separation theorem.

steps.slogan: Separate $s$ from $s^c$ by a Borel set $C$.
steps.detail: The Lusin separation theorem says that two disjoint analytic sets of a Hausdorff space are separated by a [Borel set](c:borel-set): $C$ contains the first and misses the second. Applied to $s$ and $s^c$, it gives a Borel set $C$ with $s \subseteq C$ and $C \cap s^c = \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Show that $C$ lies inside $s$.
steps.detail: The set $C$ misses $s^c$, so every point of $C$ belongs to $s$. Hence $C \subseteq s$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inclusions to get $s = C$, a Borel set.
steps.detail: The inclusions $s \subseteq C$ and $C \subseteq s$ give $s = C$. The set $C$ is Borel, so $s$ is Borel.

concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Hausdorff separation of points is what the separation theorem uses.
concepts.c:analytic-set: The two disjoint analytic sets are the input of the separation theorem.
concepts.c:borel-set: The separating set is Borel, and it turns out to equal $s$.

source.note: mathlib applies AnalyticSet.measurablySeparable to s and its complement, gets a measurable u with s contained in u and u disjoint from the complement, and shows u = s by antisymmetry.

statement: Every [partial order](c:partial-order) $\le$ on a set $X$ is contained in a [total order](c:total-order) on $X$: there is a total order $\preceq$ with $x \le y \Rightarrow x \preceq y$.

hypotheses.text: The relation $\le$ is a [partial order](c:partial-order) on the set $X$.

proofs.name: Maximal partial order
proofs.slogan: A maximal partial order above the given one is total, because two incomparable points could still be ordered.
proofs.scope: Every set $X$, using Zorn's lemma. The empty set and singletons are total already.

roles.why: The given order is the starting element of the family and a lower bound for every chain.

steps.slogan: Collect all partial orders on $X$ that contain $\le$, ordered by inclusion.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of [partial orders](c:partial-order) $s \supseteq {\le}$ on $X$. It is nonempty because $\le \in \mathcal S$, and inclusion is a partial order on $\mathcal S$.

steps.slogan: Show that the union of a nonempty chain in $\mathcal S$ is an upper bound.
steps.detail: Let $u$ be the union of a nonempty chain. It is reflexive because each member is. If $x\,u\,y$ and $y\,u\,z$, both pairs lie in members $s_1, s_2$ of the chain. The larger of them contains both pairs, so it gives $x\,z$ by transitivity. Antisymmetry is checked in the same way.

steps.slogan: Obtain a [maximal element](c:maximal-element) $s$ of $\mathcal S$ from Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Every chain of $\mathcal S$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal S$: the union for nonempty chains, and $\le$ for the empty chain. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal $s$, which is a partial order containing $\le$.

steps.slogan: Assume $x, y$ are incomparable under $s$ and define a larger relation $s'$.
steps.detail: Suppose neither $x\,s\,y$ nor $y\,s\,x$. Put $a\,s'\,b$ when $a\,s\,b$, or when $a\,s\,x$ and $y\,s\,b$. Then $s \subseteq s'$, and $x\,s'\,y$ because $x\,s\,x$ and $y\,s\,y$, while $x\,s\,y$ fails.

steps.slogan: Check that $s'$ is a partial order.
steps.detail: Reflexivity comes from $s$. Transitivity follows in the four cases from transitivity of $s$. For antisymmetry, any case that is not $a\,s\,b$ and $b\,s\,a$ gives $y\,s\,x$ through a chain such as $y\,s\,b\,s\,a\,s\,x$, which is excluded.

steps.slogan: Contradict maximality of $s$ to show that $s$ is total.
steps.detail: The relation $s'$ lies in $\mathcal S$ and strictly contains $s$, which contradicts maximality. So any two elements are comparable under $s$, and $s$ is a [total order](c:total-order) that contains $\le$.

concepts.c:partial-order: Partial orders containing the given one form the family where Zorn's lemma works.
concepts.c:total-order: A total order is the goal: every two elements are comparable.
concepts.c:maximal-element: The maximal partial order is the element that must already be total.

source.note: mathlib applies zorn_le_nonempty₀ to the partial orders above r, with sSup of a chain as upper bound, and for incomparable x, y enlarges a maximal s by the relation s x' y' or (s x' x and s y y').

statement: Let $A$ be a [closed](c:closed-set) subset of a [normal space](c:normal-space) $X$ and $f\colon A \to \mathbb{R}$ a [continuous](c:continuous-function) function. Then $f$ extends to a continuous $F\colon X \to \mathbb{R}$. If $|f| \le M$ on $A$, then $F$ can be chosen with $|F| \le M$.
conclusion: There is a continuous $F\colon X \to \mathbb{R}$ with $F|_A = f$, and $|F| \le M$ whenever $|f| \le M$.

formal.difference: The declaration treats a bounded continuous function on a space with a closed embedding into a normal space, and gives an extension of equal norm. The unbounded case is the separate declaration ContinuousMap.exists_extension.

proofs.name: Series of Urysohn approximations
proofs.slogan: Approximate the function by Urysohn functions at each stage, sum the uniformly convergent series, and treat unbounded functions through a bounded homeomorphic image.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 4 prove the bounded case with the same bound; step 5 reduces the unbounded case to it. The empty set $A$ is trivial.

roles.why: Normality lets Urysohn's lemma separate disjoint closed sets by a continuous function.
A closed subset keeps closed sets of $A$ closed in $X$, so Urysohn's lemma applies in $X$.
Continuity of $f$ makes the sets where $f$ is large closed, and keeps every error term continuous.

steps.slogan: Find a continuous function on $X$ that approximates $f$ within two thirds of its bound.
steps.detail: Assume $|f| \le c$. The sets $P = \{f \le -c/3\}$ and $Q = \{f \ge c/3\}$ are disjoint and closed in $A$, so closed in $X$. Urysohn's lemma gives continuous $g\colon X \to [-c/3, c/3]$ equal to $-c/3$ on $P$ and to $c/3$ on $Q$. Then $|f - g| \le 2c/3$ on $A$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the approximation on the error to get $g_n$ with $|g_n| \le \frac{c}{3}(2/3)^n$.
steps.detail: Put $f_0 = f$. If $|f_n| \le (2/3)^n c$ on $A$, step 1 gives $g_n$ on $X$ with $|g_n| \le \frac{c}{3}(2/3)^n$, and $f_{n+1} = f_n - g_n|_A$ satisfies $|f_{n+1}| \le (2/3)^{n+1} c$.

steps.slogan: Sum the series $G = \sum g_n$ and check that $G$ is continuous.
steps.detail: Since $\sum \frac{c}{3}(2/3)^n = c$, the Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence. A uniform sum of continuous functions is continuous, so $G$ is continuous with $|G| \le c$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G$ agrees with $f$ on $A$.
steps.detail: On $A$, $f - \sum_{k<n} g_k = f_n$ and $|f_n| \le (2/3)^n c \to 0$, so $G|_A = f$. With $c = M$ this proves the bounded case with $|G| \le M$.

steps.slogan: Reduce an unbounded $f$ to the bounded case through a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) onto $(-1, 1)$.
steps.detail: Let $\phi(t) = t/(1 + |t|)$, a homeomorphism $\mathbb{R} \to (-1, 1)$. Extend $\phi \circ f$ to $G\colon X \to [-1, 1]$. The set $D = \{|G| = 1\}$ is closed and misses $A$, so Urysohn's lemma gives $u\colon X \to [0, 1]$ with $u = 1$ on $A$ and $u = 0$ on $D$. Then $uG$ has values in $(-1, 1)$ and $F = \phi^{-1} \circ (uG)$ extends $f$.

concepts.c:closed-set: Closed sets are what Urysohn's lemma separates, and $A$ is closed.
concepts.c:normal-space: Normality is exactly the separation property that Urysohn's lemma needs.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity makes the level sets closed and keeps each approximation continuous.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The homeomorphism trades an unbounded function for a bounded one and back.

source.note: mathlib iterates tietze_extension_step (Urysohn on the sets where f is at most -|f|/3 and at least |f|/3) and takes the limit of the partial sums; step 5 is the standard reduction of unbounded functions, not part of this declaration.
